How quantum-safe is .nl?
Report Methodology Data Search

Methodology

How the weekly scan selects domains, measures their key exchange and turns handshakes into the figures in the report

1Target population

The headline figure, the trend and the hosting analysis cover the .nl domains ranked in the top 250,000 of the Tranco list, a research ranking of popular domains that combines several popularity rankings over 30 days. Each scan records the Tranco list ID, 64X5X for the latest scan, so its input can be reproduced.

The rest of the Tranco top 1 million is scanned as well and shown as a separate band. Below rank 250,000, the .nl domains include thousands of similar, apparently generated names, most of them hosted on one network. In the latest scan that part held 1 reachable domains, 100.0% of them post-quantum by default. Counting them in the main figure would make it mostly a measure of that network.

The sector comparison uses curated lists with a source for every entry, so it includes organisations whose domains are not in the Tranco list:

  • Government: ministries, provinces, municipalities, water boards, agencies, independent administrative bodies, inspectorates, High Councils of State, the judiciary and the police, taken from the Organisaties overheid register, plus national services that the register lists as part of a ministry, such as the Belastingdienst.
  • Banks, hospitals and web shops: compiled from public lists.

The lists can be downloaded from the data page. A domain can be in the Tranco list and in a sector list at the same time. Domains are lowercased and stripped of a leading www., and domains that opted out are removed before scanning.

2Measurement

For each domain the scanner connects to port 443 of the domain itself. If that does not complete a TLS handshake, it tries the www. host instead and records which host answered. It then runs up to two handshakes:

  1. Default handshake. The scanner offers what current browsers offer: the hybrid post-quantum group X25519MLKEM768 and the classic groups X25519, P-256 and P-384, over TLS 1.2 or 1.3. It records the group and TLS version the server picks, the server's IP address and its certificate.
  2. Support check. Only when the server picked a classic group: a second handshake over TLS 1.3 that offers only the hybrid groups X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024. If it succeeds, the server supports post-quantum key exchange, but a current browser does not get it.

Each connection attempt times out after 10 seconds and is retried once after a timeout. Certificates do not have to verify, so that an expired or self-signed certificate does not hide the key exchange. Whether the certificate verifies against the system roots is recorded in the raw data and does not change the status.

3Classification

StatusMeaning
Post-quantum by defaultThe default handshake used a hybrid post-quantum group. Traffic recorded today cannot be decrypted later by breaking the key exchange with a quantum computer.
Supported, not defaultThe server chose a classic group in the default handshake but completed the post-quantum-only handshake.
Classic onlyThe server used a classic group and refused the post-quantum-only handshake.
Not reachableNo TLS handshake completed on either host. These domains are left out of every percentage.

4Hosting attribution

Each server's IP address is mapped to the autonomous system that announces it, using the public-domain iptoasn.com table downloaded on the day of the scan. An autonomous system is a network run by one organisation, such as a hosting company, a cloud provider or a content delivery network. The report names networks after the organisation behind them, Cloudflare rather than CLOUDFLARENET, and always gives the AS number. A site behind a content delivery network is attributed to that network, not to the company that hosts its origin server.

5Statistical analysis

Every percentage is a share of reachable domains. Domains where no TLS handshake completed are left out of the denominator and reported in the coverage section of the report.

Intervals are 95% Wilson score intervals. They describe the uncertainty that comes from the number of domains behind an estimate, not from the choice of population or from measurement error. The Wilson interval stays within 0–100% and holds up for small groups and for shares near 0 or 100%, where the usual normal approximation fails.

Networks and sectors with fewer than 20 reachable domains are left out of the figures and the findings; below that size one domain moves the share by more than five percentage points. Percentages are rounded to one decimal.

The key findings on the report page are generated from the latest scan with fixed sentence templates. A finding is only shown when the data it describes is there, so the list can change from week to week.

7Limitations

  • Only port 443 of the domain and its www. host is checked. Redirects to other hosts are not followed, and mail servers are not measured.
  • Scans run from one location in the United States. Sites behind a content delivery network may answer differently elsewhere.
  • The scanner is written in Go. Its handshake resembles a browser's but is not identical, so a few servers may choose differently for a real browser.
  • Servers that only speak TLS 1.1 or older, or only legacy cipher suites or signatures that Go refuses, and servers that stall on the large post-quantum ClientHello, show up as not reachable rather than classic only. Because unreachable domains are left out of the percentages, this slightly raises the headline figure.
  • Only key exchange is measured, not certificates or signatures.

8Ethics and opting out

The scanner only performs TLS handshakes. It sends no application data, requests no web pages and closes each connection after the handshake. Per domain it performs at most three handshakes: the domain, its www. host only when the domain fails, and the post-quantum check only when the server chose a classic group. Each is retried once after a timeout. At most 64 connections are open at a time across all domains, and a scan runs for a few minutes once a week.

To exclude a domain from future scans, open an opt-out request on GitHub. The domain will be added to the exclusion list.
